title: Zionist Organizing, Youth, and Mutual Aid in Skala
summary: Zionist initiatives in Skala joined youth organizing and Hebrew culture with practical efforts to support neighbors.

## A movement built in the town

In Skala, Zionism was more than a political idea or a distant promise of emigration. It took shape in Hebrew lessons, youth clubs, elections, fundraising, loans for struggling families, and public farewells at the railway station. The memorial book presents these activities as parts of a shared local life, carried forward by people whose commitments could be educational, political, charitable, or all three.

The book remembers [Avi Moti Vidber](/communities/skala/records/mention_273a53dea14da2751dadb6cf) as a founder of Skala’s Zionist movement and an initiator of its first Hebrew school. It also describes a broader political presence: local Zionists won an early election to the [community council](/communities/skala/records/event_candidate_1d853413ac2e1b2b2d3cd607). These recollections place organizing inside the institutions of everyday communal life, rather than at its margins.

The memorial book’s account of Skala’s Hebrew education begins with the Tarbut school, founded in 1906, and describes later educational and cultural work in the People’s House. Its three floors brought together classrooms, a library and reading room, an auditorium, and a basement meeting place for Hashomer Hatzair. The memorial book places these institutions in a town where Jewish education also included traditional religious learning and Polish public schooling. It recalls [Yisrael-Leib Freifelder](/communities/skala/records/mention_de39ae7eb2180a83cc3dfad2) as a Bible teacher at an evening school, alongside other local educators. The wider civic setting is visible in the record of the [People’s House](/communities/skala/records/mention_864b36e478be14ec9df05ebd); its exact founding date differs between accounts, so it is safer to say it was established in the early 1920s than to assign a single year.

## Youth groups, different paths

Zionist youth activity was not one uniform organization. The memorial book names Hashomer Hatzair, Gordonia, Buslia, Hanoar Hatzioni, and Betar, whose members met, debated, and sometimes disagreed over the Zionist movement and events in Palestine. Religious Zionists, by contrast, are described as supporting the Mizrachi list during Zionist Congress elections without maintaining a local organization or youth movement of their own. That distinction matters: Skala’s Zionist life included competing outlooks, not simply a single united campaign.

The book’s account connects youth activity with practical preparation for emigration. Members raised money for the Jewish National Fund and sought immigration certificates for those who had completed *hachshara*—agricultural training intended to prepare pioneers for work in Palestine. A separate account of the local [HeHalutz branch](/communities/skala/records/event_candidate_1cf9e981b9d9d8aa7ba88234) describes organizing local youth; another record names [Mordechai Fingerman](/communities/skala/records/mention_6cd5d120a039258edc162ac3), an immigrant from Russia who helped Skala residents pursue aliyah. The memorial book says that departing pioneers were accompanied to the railway station in public processions. It remembers this as a town-wide occasion, not merely a private departure.

The local group belonged to a larger regional and international world. Hashomer Hatzair originated in Galicia in the early twentieth century, and the movement’s combination of youth education, scouting, socialist ideas, and Zionist aims helps explain why its Skala branch could be both a club and a formative social environment. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum describes how Jewish youth movements in Poland later sustained networks and leadership under wartime persecution; that broader history gives context, but it does not establish what any particular Skala member did during the Holocaust. ([USHMM, “Jewish Youth Movements in Wartime Poland”](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/jewish-youth-movements-in-wartime-poland-from-minority-to-leadership))

## Aid as part of public life

The memorial book also remembers Zionist leaders’ involvement in institutions that addressed immediate need. It records the founding of a [Gemilut Hasadim loan fund](/communities/skala/records/event_candidate_8e366b123145c3c1e3011ec4), which provided loans to people with limited means, and a [People’s Bank](/communities/skala/records/event_candidate_5aca7fa41904fd3af0e5388c), established with help from the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee. These were different responses to hardship: interest-free or charitable lending on one hand, and a banking institution supported by outside funds on the other.

The book identifies [Mordechai (Moti) Weidberg](/communities/skala/records/mention_a53135494a2632087f0a8378) with the Gemilut Hasadim fund and names [Matie Weidberg](/communities/skala/records/mention_13ecb42032a15103fccc0de3) and [Moshe Feirstein](/communities/skala/records/mention_605ba53e4ea95f3c44b7a554) among public figures associated with support for HeHalutz. The memorial account describes lending institutions as a significant source of help, but it does not let us calculate precisely how many households benefited or assign every initiative to one person. Elsewhere it remembers additional welfare activity, including aid to the sick. In this setting, communal assistance and Zionist organizing were not opposites: practical help at home could coexist with fundraising and plans to build a future elsewhere.

## Memory, evidence, and what remains unresolved

The memorial book was written by survivors and former residents seeking to preserve a community devastated by the Holocaust. Its testimony gives names and meaning to Skala’s organizations, but it is not a complete register of everyone who belonged, emigrated, or suffered. Its recollections of departures and institutions should be read as community memory, especially where dates and details vary.

Independent records add useful checks. Yad Vashem’s town entry identifies Skala with its Polish and Yiddish forms and records 1,555 Jewish residents among a population of 4,017 in the 1921 census. It confirms the larger local setting, not the details of each organization or individual story. ([Yad Vashem, “Skala, Poland”](https://collections.yadvashem.org/en/places/5440531)) A separately preserved 1938 Keren Hayesod application, signed by Moses and Leiser Wasserman of Skala, offers documentary evidence that at least some residents participated in fundraising for the Zionist project; it is not a translation of the memorial book, nor proof of the scale of local membership. ([Skala Research Group, “Skala and the International Zionist Movement”](https://kehilalinks.jewishgen.org/skalapodol/ZionistApplication.html))

The movement’s work in Skala thus joined education, youth culture, mutual aid, and emigration planning without erasing differences among Zionist groups or between Zionists and their opponents. Some residents prepared to leave; others organized institutions that helped neighbors remain afloat. The memorial book preserves both impulses as part of the same communal history. The fate of many named activists is bound to the destruction of Skala’s Jewish community, while the sources available here do not resolve every person’s later path. Further research into the local [HeHalutz training network](research:Skala HeHalutz members and agricultural training) and the records of emigrating families may extend what can be known.
